pages.title: Synchronous vs Asynchronous Network Models
bulletPoints: Formal distributed models: Graph G = (V, E) of independent automata communicating via message passing.
Synchronous networks: Global clock rounds; messages sent at round r arrive before round r+1.
Asynchronous networks: Arbitrary non-zero message delays; no global clock; relative event ordering via causality.
Complexity measures: Time complexity (rounds or time units) vs Message complexity (total network messages exchanged).

pages.title: Leader Election in Rings
bulletPoints: The Leader Election problem: Exactly one process enters the LEADER state; all others enter NON-LEADER state.
LeLann-Chang-Roberts (LCR) algorithm: Unidirectional ring; processes forward higher IDs; O(n^2) message complexity.
Hirschberg-Sinclair (HS) algorithm: Bidirectional ring; doubling search neighborhoods yielding O(n log n) messages.
Lower bounds: Omega(n log n) messages required for comparison-based election in anonymous and general rings.

pages.title: Breadth-First Search (BFS) & Shortest Path Trees
bulletPoints: BFS tree construction in synchronous networks: Layer-by-layer exploration in O(diam) rounds.
Asynchronous BFS: Managing synchronization barriers and token propagation over arbitrary latency edges.
Shortest path tree algorithms: Bellman-Ford distributed shortest paths with message complexity O(n * m).
Applications of distributed BFS trees: Broadcasting, message routing, network diameter estimation.

pages.title: Minimum Spanning Trees: Gallager-Humblet-Spira (GHS)
bulletPoints: Distributed MST problem: Constructing minimum weight spanning tree without centralized coordinator.
Fragment concept: Disjoint tree fragments finding minimum-weight outgoing edges (MWOE) concurrently.
GHS algorithm execution: Merging fragments of equal level or absorbing lower-level fragments.
Complexity guarantees: Optimal O(n log n + m) messages and O(n log n) time across general asynchronous networks.

pages.title: Logical Time & Lamport Clocks
bulletPoints: The limitations of physical clocks: Clock drift, skew, and relativistic latency in distributed systems.
Lamport's Happened-Before Relation (->): Defining causal ordering of internal events and message send/receive pairs.
Lamport Scalar Logical Clocks: Monotonically increasing counters C(a) < C(b) if a -> b.
Total ordering: Breaking ties with unique process IDs to achieve consistent distributed event sequencing.

pages.title: Vector Clocks & Causal Consistency
bulletPoints: Limitation of scalar clocks: C(a) < C(b) does NOT imply a caused b (cannot detect concurrent independent events).
Vector Clock representation: Vector V_i where V_i[j] represents process i's knowledge of process j's clock.
Vector clock update rules: Increment local index upon local event; take component-wise maximum upon message receipt.
Causal ordering: Event a -> b if and only if V(a) <= V(b) and V(a) != V(b); detecting concurrent conflicts in replicas.

pages.title: Distributed Mutual Exclusion: Lamport & Ricart-Agrawala
bulletPoints: Mutual exclusion requirement: Safety (at most one process in CS), Liveness (no starvation), Fairness.
Lamport's Mutual Exclusion Algorithm: Request queues ordered by Lamport timestamps; requires 3(n - 1) messages.
Ricart-Agrawala optimization: Eliminating explicit RELEASE messages; deferred OK replies yielding 2(n - 1) messages.
Token-based algorithms: Suzuki-Kasami token-passing protocol requiring at most n messages per critical section entry.

pages.title: Global State & The Chandy-Lamport Snapshot
bulletPoints: Consistent Global Snapshot: A cut where for every event e in the cut, all causal predecessors of e are also in the cut.
The Chandy-Lamport snapshot algorithm: Recording local process states and in-flight channel messages.
Marker sending and receiving rules: Incoming markers delineate channel recording boundaries.
Applications: Checkpointing for disaster recovery, distributed deadlock detection, and termination detection.

pages.title: Consensus in Synchronous Systems
bulletPoints: The Consensus Problem: Agreement (all non-faulty decide same value), Validity (value decided was proposed), Termination.
Crash failures vs Byzantine (arbitrary/malicious) failures.
Crash failure consensus: Flooding algorithm reaching consensus in f + 1 rounds where f is max crash failures.
Lower bound proof: Any consensus algorithm tolerating f crash failures requires at least f + 1 synchronous rounds.

pages.title: Byzantine Agreement in Synchronous Systems
bulletPoints: Byzantine Generals Problem: Traitors sending conflicting messages to different loyal generals.
The 3m + 1 requirement: Proving consensus is impossible with 3 generals and 1 traitor (need at least 4 generals).
Oral Message algorithm OM(m): Recursive algorithm reaching agreement with 3m + 1 nodes and m Byzantine traitors.
Signed messages (SM(m)): Using unforgeable digital signatures to reduce node requirement to 2m + 1.

pages.title: The FLP Impossibility Theorem
bulletPoints: Fischer, Lynch, and Paterson (1985) landmark theorem in theoretical computer science.
Theorem statement: In an asynchronous network, no deterministic consensus protocol can guarantee termination even with a single crash failure.
Bivalent vs Univalent configurations: Proving the existence of an infinite non-terminating execution path.
Circumventing FLP: Partial synchrony (timing assumptions), randomized algorithms, and failure detectors.

pages.title: Failure Detectors: Chandra and Toueg
bulletPoints: Abstracting time: Decoupling consensus logic from network timeout heuristics via Failure Detectors.
Completeness: Eventually every crashed process is permanently suspected by every non-faulty process.
Accuracy: Strong accuracy (no correct process is ever suspected) vs Weak accuracy.
The Eventually Strong Detector (Diamond-S): The weakest failure detector needed to solve consensus in asynchronous networks.

pages.title: The Paxos Consensus Protocol: Synod
bulletPoints: Leslie Lamport's Paxos: The foundation of fault-tolerant distributed databases and consensus engines.
Roles: Proposers (advocating values), Acceptors (voting consensus memory), Learners (discovering decided values).
Phase 1 (Prepare / Promise): Proposer broadcasts Prepare(n); Acceptors promise not to accept proposals < n and return highest accepted.
Phase 2 (Accept / Accepted): Proposer sends Accept(n, v); Acceptors accept proposal if no promise broken; consensus committed.

pages.title: Multi-Paxos: High-Throughput Log Replication
bulletPoints: The cost of Basic Paxos: 2 network round-trips for every single committed value.
Multi-Paxos optimization: Electing a stable leader to execute Phase 1 once for an infinite stream of log slots.
Steady-state operation: Phase 2 only (1 RTT commit) streaming log entries to majority acceptor quorums.
Leader changeover: Executing Phase 1 over uncommitted log slots to reconcile conflicting state.

pages.title: The Raft Consensus Algorithm
bulletPoints: Designed for understandability: Decomposing consensus into Leader Election, Log Replication, and Safety.
Leader election: Randomized election timeouts, RequestVote RPCs, and majority quorum terms.
Log replication: AppendEntries RPCs with consistency checks (prevLogIndex, prevLogTerm); heartbeats enforce leader authority.
Log Matching Invariant: If two logs contain an entry with same index and term, they are identical up to that index.

pages.title: Byzantine Fault Tolerance: PBFT
bulletPoints: Practical Byzantine Fault Tolerance (Castro & Liskov 1999): High-performance BFT in asynchronous networks.
System requirement: 3f + 1 total replicas to tolerate f arbitrary Byzantine faulty nodes.
Three-phase protocol: Pre-Prepare (leader assigns sequence number), Prepare (2f matching votes), Commit (2f+1 commit votes).
View Change protocol: Replacing malicious or dead leaders through signed cryptographic state certificates.

pages.title: Gossip Protocols & Epidemic Algorithms
bulletPoints: Decentralized peer-to-peer dissemination modeled after biological epidemic disease propagation.
Anti-entropy vs Rumor mongering: Comparing complete state digests vs pushing hot updates to random peers.
Mathematical scaling: Information reaches N nodes in O(log N) rounds with high probability.
Use cases: Cluster membership in Cassandra, failure detection in Consul, and gossip networks in Ethereum.

pages.title: Distributed Hash Tables (DHT): Chord
bulletPoints: Peer-to-peer lookup service: Mapping keys to nodes on an identifier circle modulo 2^m.
Consistent hashing: Key k is assigned to first node whose identifier is >= k (successor(k)).
Finger tables: Routing tables with m entries storing successor(n + 2^(i-1)) for O(log N) lookup hops.
Node join and stabilization: Concurrent maintenance of predecessor and successor pointers under high churn.

pages.title: Kademlia & XOR Metric Routing
bulletPoints: XOR metric: Distance d(x, y) = x XOR y satisfying all mathematical metric space properties (triangle inequality).
k-buckets: Routing tables partitioned into logarithmic distance ranges tracking live peer contact info.
Lookup algorithm: Iteratively querying alpha closest nodes to target key, converging in O(log N) steps.
Real-world deployments: The backbone of BitTorrent Mainline DHT and Ethereum node discovery (discv5).

pages.title: Self-Stabilizing Distributed Systems
bulletPoints: Edsger Dijkstra's self-stabilization concept: A system that converges to a legitimate state from any arbitrary initial state.
Transient fault tolerance: Recovering automatically from memory corruption, power glitches, and illegal states.
Self-stabilizing token ring: Dijkstra's K-state machine algorithm guaranteeing single-token circulation.
Convergence and Closure: Proving execution paths enter legitimate states and remain within legitimate states.

pages.title: Distributed Commit: 2PC vs 3PC
bulletPoints: Atomic commit: Guaranteeing all participating database shards commit or abort a transaction together.
Two-Phase Commit (2PC): Blocking coordinator vulnerability when coordinator crashes during commit phase.
Three-Phase Commit (3PC): Introducing Pre-Commit state to enable non-blocking recovery in crash-stop networks.
Why 3PC fails in partitions: Network partitions can cause split-brain commits, which is why Paxos/Raft are preferred.

pages.title: Distributed Shared Memory & Consistency Models
bulletPoints: Strict Consistency: All writes are instantaneously visible to all readers across the universe (physically impossible).
Sequential Consistency (Lamport): Results of execution are equivalent to some serial order respecting each process's program order.
Linearizability (Herlihy & Wing): Strongest practical consistency; operations take effect atomically at a linearization point between invocation and response.
Eventual Consistency: If no new updates are made, all replicas will eventually converge to identical values.

pages.title: CRDTs: Conflict-Free Replicated Data Types
bulletPoints: Optimistic replication without consensus: Replicas accept local concurrent writes without network coordination.
State-based CRDTs (CvRDTs): Replicas exchange entire states and merge using mathematical join-semilattices (commutative, associative, idempotent).
Operation-based CRDTs (CmRDTs): Replicas broadcast update operations over reliable causal channels.
Types of CRDTs: PN-Counters, LWW-Element-Set, OR-Set (Observed-Remove Set), and Sequence CRDTs (RGA/Automerge) for collaborative text.

pages.title: Distributed Deadlock Detection Algorithms
bulletPoints: Wait-for graphs across distributed nodes: Identifying distributed resource dependency cycles.
Chandy-Misra-Haas edge-chasing algorithm: Circulating probe messages (initiator, sender, receiver) along wait-for edges.
Priority-based optimization: Only higher-priority processes launch probes to prevent message flooding.
False deadlocks: Phantom deadlocks detected because of asynchronous message delays reporting obsolete wait conditions.

pages.title: Synthesis of Distributed Algorithmic Foundations
bulletPoints: The unifying themes: Time, causality, fault models, agreement, and state machine replication.
The trade-off frontier: CAP theorem, PACELC theorem, latency vs consistency, and message complexity.
From theory to practice: How theoretical bounds govern modern cloud datacenters, blockchains, and global databases.
Mastery checkpoint: Designing resilient, provably correct distributed protocols for the next century of computing.
